## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a machine that completes every trial still lack the evidence to be allowed among people?_

A successful trial shows what a machine did under the conditions it happened to meet, while permission to operate is a claim about every condition it may meet next. Thousands of clean runs on a dry floor say nothing about the stop on a floor no trial touched, and a brake that stopped the machine last month may not stop it inside the same distance after its lining wears. A machine granted authority on demonstrations therefore carries untested premises into service, where the first test of each one is the event it was meant to prevent. Deciding to deploy requires stating which physical claims the evidence supports, under which conditions and for how long, refusing or narrowing operation wherever a premise remains unknown, and withdrawing the grant when brakes wear, sensors shift, or software changes. At the causal boundary, authority must expire when its physical justification does, because a later software correction cannot undo motion already produced.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a claim-argument-evidence (CAE) safety case as an auditable engineering assertion DAG linking bounded operating envelopes to empirical hardware evidence
- Grade each claim's premises as measured, datasheet, illustrative, or unknown, and select the verdict (`UNCOND`, `COND`, or `REFUSE`) they support
- Join task-success, cycle-time, and intervention evidence to the physical measurements and restrictions supporting a conditional release
- Specify standing-condition cadences and validated responses separately from the execution leases that bound individual action chunks
- Diagnose unsupported warrants, hidden contextual assumptions, and compound defeaters through adversarial review of a release argument
- Specify the records a release manifest binds by digest and the conditions under which its gate refuses motion
- Determine which claims a policy or software update reopens, and why shadow operation cannot substitute for closed-loop qualification

:::
## The Decision to Deploy {#sec-release-decision-to-deploy}

Every machine operating among humans eventually crosses a release threshold: the point where builders formally grant it authority to act outside the laboratory. In conventional software engineering, deployment is largely reversible; an operator can recall a defective build within minutes, bounding the cost of failure to the time required to roll back the binary. For physical systems, that release grant differs fundamentally. Every action authorized by the runtime delivers energy across the causal boundary into the physical environment. When a release decision errs, the failure manifests as an actuator driving past an obstacle clearance line or a gripper exerting uncalibrated force against human tissue, and no software rollback can recall kinetic energy already transferred. Aerospace, rail transit, and industrial robotics manage this gravity through an explicit safety case—a structured, auditable argument detailing what the machine is claimed to do, under what specific operational conditions, and backed by what concrete evidence. Physical AI inherits this rigorous burden while confronting an acute difficulty: a learned policy cannot be proven safe through static structural inspection, and finite field trials can never exhaustively surface the rare tail-distribution failures that carry catastrophic consequences.

A release decision determines which operational claims the available evidence actually licenses, under what physical conditions, and for how long. Rather than reducing deployment readiness to a single benchmark metric, robust engineering treats deployment as a bounded, revocable adjudication. The argument begins by defining a bounded operational envelope and explicitly mapping every physical claim to concrete verification artifacts. That adjudication yields one of three outcomes: full operational authorization, restricted operation with enforced boundary limits, or an outright refusal to deploy. Crucially, standing conditions define the exact criteria under which that authorization expires. An adversarial review challenges the safety claims, an explicit adjudication resolves competing evidence, and a signed deployment manifest binds the final decision to the executing machine—ensuring that every subsequent software update, retrained weight checkpoint, or hardware modification must traverse the same release gate.

The warehouse mobile manipulator illustrates why past operational success cannot single-handedly license deployment. Consider a platform deployed to an active logistics depot: it must transit narrow aisles past protruding shelf ends, unseat a spring-latched maintenance cage, and hand a ceramic mug to a human coworker. Each subtask hinges on an entirely distinct physical claim—guaranteed stopping distance within dynamic clearance limits at maximum payload, bounded peak force during mechanical latch manipulation, and strictly limited contact forces during collaborative handoffs. A spotless test run demonstrates only that the machine executed those motions under the exact conditions encountered during that single trial. A defensible release decision must instead establish the distribution of physical variations the machine will face in production, certifying that verified system dynamics and low-level safety interlocks bound operational risk across that entire envelope.

Hardware and software verification establishes how the system behaves when stressed by timing jitter, CAN bus contention, and sensor dropouts under injected faults (@sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection). Those verification records pair observed traces against predeclared test oracles while explicitly cataloging untested failure modes. However, laboratory fault injection alone does not constitute an operational safety argument. Engineers must systematically determine the envelope within which that empirical evidence guarantees bounded behavior. High offline validation accuracy (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics) and spotless laboratory demonstrations (@sec-verification-fault-injection) provide necessary baseline confidence, but neither establishes deployment safety. Releasing an embodied system demands an auditable adjudication demonstrating that empirical test artifacts strictly bound physical operational risk across the named operational design domain.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The empirical verification evidence backing release claims is produced in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

A system deployment must deliver useful work alongside safety within its certified envelope. Closed-loop evaluation logs (@sec-evaluation-logs) document whether an end-to-end policy achieves its operational goals, quantify human intervention rates, and isolate environmental conditions that trigger policy breakdown. Engineers must assess these operational metrics directly against the velocity limits, payload caps, and spatial restrictions mandated by the safety case. An autonomous platform that repeatedly triggers safety stops to prevent collisions avoids physical damage but achieves zero throughput. Conversely, an agile policy that demonstrates high task completion in nominal settings cannot be granted actuator authority until deterministic guardrails enforce fail-safe bounds during perception anomalies. The release decision synthesizes these complementary demands into a unified operational profile.

Because operating environments introduce distinct lighting, floor friction, and human traffic dynamics, an initial release case targets a single operational facility. Cryptographically signed fault records (@sec-verification-fault-manifest) document system behavior under explicit fault modes, while physical criteria draw on site clearance surveys, maximum-payload braking trials, and calibrated impact force measurements. Systems engineers must map each empirical record to its corresponding safety claim while transparently documenting any unverified assumptions. Before linking evidence to claims, however, engineers must formalize the claims themselves as testable physical criteria that the system either conclusively satisfies or demonstrably violates.
## The Deployment Authorization Criterion {#sec-release-question}

At a rack end, the base must stop inside the available clearance. During handover, the arm must stay within the assessed contact-force limit. Both claims depend on the response arriving before its deadline. These requirements give release authorization testable physical criteria:
$$d_{\text{stop}}(v, \tau_{\text{delay}}, a_{\text{brake}}, \delta_{\text{loc}}, \epsilon_{\text{track}}) \le D_{\text{clear}}, \quad F_{\text{contact}}(v, m_{\text{eff}}, k_H) \le F_{\text{limit}}, \quad T_{\text{exec}} \le T_{\text{deadline}}.$$ {#eq-release-authorization-criterion}

Because each criterion is a physical inequality, release authorization cannot rest on intuition, demonstrations, or aggregate benchmark scores. Authorizing deployment requires an auditable safety argument that links every inequality to measured observation ages, worst-case execution time bounds, empirical braking and contact trials, and a validated fallback. Furthermore, these physical bounds inherit the individual machine's calibration—including its camera and lidar sensor transforms, joint encoder zero-offsets, and motor torque constants. A lost or drifted calibration invalidates the certified stopping budget even when software binaries remain unchanged.

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the release question asks whether empirical and analytical evidence satisfies these criteria for each of its three tasks inside a scoped operating envelope. The release case defines the assessed physical bounds, the specified hardware fault model, and the validated permission and fallback ladder. This argument justifies granting revocable tracking authority while those physical conditions hold; finite test runs cannot establish protection against uncharacterized or unmodeled hazards (\ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}).

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-contact-premises
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONTACT PREMISES INHERITED FROM THE ENFORCEMENT RECORD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: every contact number this chapter quotes (@sec-release-question,
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard, @sec-release-case-worked-full). The
# │          derivation is taught in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact.
# │ Goal:    read the contact premises exactly as the enforcement chapter
# │          derives them, so release adjudicates and never re-derives.
# │ Show:    nothing directly; the release cells below read this class.
# │ How:     mirrors calc-enforcement-contact-force (EnforcementContactForce)
# │          line for line: same MLSysIM functions, same registry inputs, same
# │          guards. Chapters render in separate kernels, so the class is
# │          rebuilt here; the identical guards make any drift between the
# │          two chapters fail the build. Edit both cells together.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_reduced_mass,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_transient_contact_speed_limit,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementContactForce:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (guarded approach)
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    k_latch = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative
    t_contact = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (contact loop)
    f_lim = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived
    m_hand = AISLE.m_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    k_hand = AISLE.k_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    f_contact = AISLE.f_contact_criterion  # category: chosen
    v_handover = AISLE.v_handover  # category: chosen (handover approach under accept_item)
    tcp_limit = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen (free-space TCP limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    stop_lo = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch, scenario=AISLE)
    stop_hi = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch_high, scenario=AISLE)
    df_dt = stop_lo["df_dt"]
    f_cmd = stop_lo["f_at_brake_onset"]
    x_rem = stop_lo["x_remaining"]
    a_arm = stop_lo["a_arm_needed"]
    t_arm_stop = stop_lo["t_arm_stop"]
    f_cmd_hi = stop_hi["f_at_brake_onset"]
    a_arm_hi = stop_hi["a_arm_needed"]
    m_red = calc_reduced_mass(m_eff, m_hand).to(kilogram)
    f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(tcp_limit, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / f_contact).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_handover_clamped = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand).to(newton)
    v_ceiling = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(meter / second)
    v_ceiling_clamped = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand).to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (identical to calc-enforcement-contact-force) ─────────────
    check(abs(f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, guarded approach, is 39 N.")
    check(abs(x_rem.to(millimeter).magnitude - 0.1525) < 5e-5, "Remaining latch compression is 0.15 mm.")
    check(abs(a_arm.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, "The guarded stop needs about 3 m/s^2 (2.95).")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.to(millisecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "The guarded stop takes about 10 ms.")
    check(abs(f_cmd_hi.to(newton).magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, unsupported approach, is 95 N.")
    check(abs(a_arm_hi.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, "The unsupported approach needs 400 m/s^2.")
    check(f_cmd < f_lim and f_cmd_hi < f_lim, "Both approaches reach brake onset below the latch limit.")
    check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Arm effective contact mass is 12.0 kg.")
    check(abs(m_red.magnitude - 0.5714) < 5e-5, "Hand-arm reduced mass is 0.571 kg.")
    check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit is 207 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N.")
    check(f_handover < f_contact < f_handover_clamped, "Transient passes and clamped fails the criterion.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Free-hand ceiling is 0.24 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand ceiling is 0.053 m/s.")
    check(v_ceiling_clamped < v_handover < v_ceiling, "The handover cap sits between the clamped and free-hand ceilings.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Raw quantities only; each release cell formats what it quotes.
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-operating-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S OPERATING ENVELOPE FOR RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (envelope and conditional-zone paragraphs),
# │          @tbl-16-odd-invariants, the contact-criteria paragraph after it, and
# │          the binding-contract paragraphs of @sec-release-three-verdicts, and
# │          the empirical-sufficiency probe of @sec-release-adversarial-review.
# │ Goal: Scope the release case to the running machine's operating envelope.
# │ Show: aisle speed and its ceiling, tote-rack payload, the friction bands and
# │       the inspected-floor ceiling, the clear distance, the latch and handover
# │       speeds with their limits, the slow-downs before a takeover, and the
# │       restricted speed on inspected floors.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; ceilings from calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity (the
# │      jerk-limited S-curve stop; jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's
# │      peak jerk at the drive limit) and the three overheads; mu_min = a_brake/g.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_mass, fmt_force, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
v_restricted = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: chosen (scenario assumption: restricted mode on inspected floors, the value @sec-frontier uses)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: ceilings and friction bands ───────────────────────────────────
# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
v_ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
a_inspected = min(AISLE.a_brake, (AISLE.mu_inspected_floor * g_std).to(meter / second**2))
v_inspected_ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_inspected, j_brake, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
# Handover ceilings are enforcement premises (calc-release-contact-premises).
v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Unconditional aisle speed ceiling is 1.44 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_aisle < v_ceiling, "Chosen aisle speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor is 0.204")
check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
check(mu_min > AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, "Inspected floor requires speed restriction")
check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Restricted ceiling on inspected floors is 1.23 m/s")
check(abs(a_inspected.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 1.1768) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor deceleration mu*g is 1.18 m/s^2")
check(a_inspected < AISLE.a_brake, "The inspected floor, not the brake, caps the deceleration")
check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling, "Chosen restricted mode sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Transient (free-hand) handover ceiling is 0.24 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its transient ceiling")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand handover ceiling is 0.053 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover > v_handover_ceiling_clamped, "Chosen handover speed exceeds the clamped ceiling, so clamping must be excluded")
check(abs(RM.loaded_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, "Running-machine loaded mass is 368 kg")
check(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop < AISLE.v_aisle, "Slow-down before an in-loop takeover")
check(AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_inspected_floor < mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Friction bands are ordered")
check(abs(AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Signed aisle speed 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude - 1.10) < 1e-9, "Clear distance 1.10 m")
check(
    abs(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-9,
    "In-loop takeover slow-down 0.75 m/s (Delta_da-charged ceiling, rounded down)",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Out-of-loop takeover slow-down 0.15 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Permission tick 1 ms")
check(AISLE.t_tick < AISLE.t_lease, "Servo tick sits inside the chunk lease")
check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is 50 kg")
check(
    abs(AISLE.mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_oil_film - 0.05) < 1e-9,
    "Friction bands 0.60, 0.12, 0.05",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded latch approach 0.03 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Unsupported latch approach 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Latch tripwire 15 N")
check(abs(AISLE.t_contact_response.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Contact-loop response 2 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit 100 N")
check(abs(AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Handover speed 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Handover criterion 50 N")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseEnvelope:
    v_restricted = v_restricted  # chosen; read by calc-release-worked-verdict
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_out_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_oil_film, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    a_inspected_str = fmt_acceleration(a_inspected, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    g_str = fmt_acceleration(g_std, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
```

A release case is scoped by the operating envelope: the target operational design domain (ODD)\index{Operational design domain!release envelope} paired with the machine's internal hardware, thermal, and timing invariants. Deployment release authorizes a system configuration under standing operating conditions, complementing rather than replacing the short execution leases that bound individual action chunks. Site inspections, calibration checks, and per-tick permission checks operate at the distinct cadences dictated by their respective failure mechanisms. An unconditional (`UNCOND`) verdict authorizes tracking proposals across the full verified operating envelope (@sec-verification-operating-envelope), a conditional (`COND`) verdict restricts operation to a designated subset with constrained kinematics or environmental fences, and a refusal (`REFUSE`) denies tracking permission entirely.\index{Operational design domain!release verdicts} For the mobile manipulator, the nominal operating envelope admits aisle travel up to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) with the tote rack loaded to at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, on floors surveyed to a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str`, and past rack ends with at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` of clear distance. For manipulation, it admits door approaches at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str` and coworker handovers at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str`.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operational design domain and its known absences are defined in @sec-data-policy-coverage.
:::

Inside these boundaries, the learned neural policy proposes actions across the nominal task envelope, but every proposed action requires independent, per-tick permission from an isolated safety enforcer. Mode-specific conditions (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) narrow that envelope. The takeover analysis evaluates candidate intervention speeds, screening an in-loop request at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` and an out-of-loop crawl at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str`; neither candidate qualifies as a standalone release limit. The moving in-loop braking blend fails its clearance check, so the base executes its resident stop before transferring control authority (@sec-intervention-authority-transitions). The restricted mode of a `COND` verdict narrows the envelope further: on a floor characterized solely through the site inspection regime, the machine runs at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` inspected-floor ceiling, while still charging dispatch-to-admission delay and maintaining a positive stopping reserve.

The rules in @tbl-16-odd-invariants follow a strict priority ladder: refusal conditions override mode-specific restrictions, which in turn override nominal limits. Because speed ranges overlap across operational contexts, these thresholds define operating modes rather than disjoint numerical intervals. For instance, a payload estimate that has gone stale since the last pick permits separately supported stationary arm work, whereas an invalid estimate or measured overload invokes the hard refusal rule. A conditional state restricts admitted proposals through enforcer clamping. A refusal state revokes the capability token, withdraws motor tracking permission, and commands a validated fallback trajectory (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder). Onboard wheel slip estimation cannot provide prospective clearance guarantees because it detects low friction only *after* traction has already been lost. A thin film of clear oil ($\mu \approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) can be visually indistinguishable from dry concrete to the navigation cameras. By the time a loaded base moving at aisle speed (`{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`) initiates braking on an oil patch and measures slip, it has already committed to a stopping distance that exceeds the clear distance. Consequently, floor friction must be guaranteed prospectively through periodic site surveys and active spill maintenance.

Sensor mounting drift degrades the localization allowance $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ over operational life even when software binaries remain unchanged (@sec-release-calibration-drift). A firmware update that overwrites measured sensor extrinsics and joint offsets\index{Over-the-air update!calibration retention} invalidates the budget just as decisively, requiring the deployment pipeline to preserve and re-verify calibration records before restoring tracking authority (@sec-release-modular-safety-cases).

The safety case must also document machine behavior when operation encounters an envelope boundary. Event-triggered edge telemetry\index{Edge telemetry!event-triggered buffer}\index{Black-box recorder!pre- and post-trigger capture} freezes circular buffer traces for post-incident review (@sec-release-data-curation-flywheel), while the deterministic permission path enforces physical boundaries in real time. @Tbl-16-odd-invariants summarizes the physical dimensions maintained by runtime monitors and administrative site controls. Internal environmental conditions from @sec-verification-operating-envelope, such as ambient temperature, DC bus rail voltage, and compute SoC utilization, enter the release case through fault injection and stress tests conducted across their qualified ranges.

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Envelope Dimension / Invariant | Nominal Envelope ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}$)                                                                           | Conditional Boundary ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}$)                                                                                                                                                                                 | Hard Refusal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}$)                                                                                                                                                         | Runtime Monitor & Rate                                                                 | Enforcer Action & Latency                                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Aisle Speed**                | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`                                                                             | Preliminary takeover screens: `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` in-loop and `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str` out-of-loop; rejected in-loop blend requires stop first                                         | Measured speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str`), or invalid speed estimate                                                   | Encoders and IMU, every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick          | Clamp admitted speed; refuse above the signed speed                            |
| **Floor Friction**             | Surveyed $\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` (dry concrete near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`)         | Qualified assessment and maintained site regime ($\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`): restricted `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling | Unsurveyed floor or reported film; a clear oil film ($\mu\approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) can evade the installed cameras                                                               | Floor survey and site spill procedure; no on-board measurement                         | Restrict speed by floor zone; refuse the aisle                                 |
| **Tote-Rack Payload**          | $0\le m\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, valid load estimate (total at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.m1_str`) | Estimate stale since the last pick: stationary arm tasks only                                                                                                                                                                        | Load above capacity or invalid estimate                                                                                                                                                                | Rack load cells, at each pick                                                          | Refuse aisle transit until re-weighed                                          |
| **Rack-End Clearance**         | Surveyed $D_{\text{clear}}\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` at every rack end                                   | Shorter surveyed clearance: lower signed speed from the same budget                                                                                                                                                                  | Unsurveyed rack end, or obstacle inside the clear distance                                                                                                                                             | Site survey; lidar and navigation camera at frame rate                                 | Speed limit per rack end; stop for a detected obstacle                         |
| **Door Latch Approach**        | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str`, strike plate at its nominal position                                       | Original policy: nominal plate only; changed recovery candidate needs its own evaluation and release case                                                                                                                            | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_high_str` approach or plate condition outside the selected policy case                                                                                               | Arm contact-force sensing in the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_contact_str` contact loop | Trip at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_trip_str`; refuse the unsupported approach |
| **Coworker Handover**          | TCP speed $\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                             | Coworker present without `accept_item`: hold short of the handover point                                                                                                                                                             | TCP speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` (transient ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`), or a clamping geometry outside the assessed transient case | Joint encoders every permission tick; arm contact-force sensing                        | Clamp TCP speed; refuse above the signed speed                                 |

: **Operating envelope of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Refusal rules take priority over restricted-mode rules and nominal limits. Conditional operation requires every relied-on premise to remain supported; stale payload evidence permits only separately supported stationary work, while an invalid estimate or overload refuses. The takeover speeds are preliminary screens, not qualified motion limits. The displayed speed ceilings are partial calculations before dispatch-to-admission delay; signed limits require that delay and a positive reserve. Sensor rates and stopping response are plant validation obligations. {#tbl-16-odd-invariants tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

The nominal latch row in @tbl-16-odd-invariants scopes the baseline policy release case. Although the separately stipulated recovery campaign in @sec-evaluation evaluates a changed candidate across nominal and displaced-plate conditions, that experimental provenance does not silently extend the contact-force or timing bounds established here. Deploying the recovery policy requires its own evaluation and safety case update.

A defensible release claim must specify its plant dynamics, assumed contact geometry, and modeled fault set. The release case for the mobile manipulator rests on three criteria: the base stops inside the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance before reaching a pedestrian stepping out at a rack end, the arm unlatches the door without exceeding the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_latch_limit_str` structural limit, and an item handover does not exceed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_contact_str` of peak contact force against the coworker. The base's stopping claim assumes a stationary obstacle; an individual walking toward the moving machine violates this relative-velocity bound and must be managed by site crossing protocols (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). A complete release argument demonstrates which human contacts are excluded before impact, which detected contacts fall within the compliance model, and which single-point faults trigger the isolated fallback. Halting motion after impact occurs does not reduce the initial shock force.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-biomechanical-impact-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HANDOVER CONTACT FORCE AND THE BASE'S STOPPING SPARE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (the handover-premise paragraph and the
# │          spare-spent-as-delay paragraph), and the refusal paragraph of
# │          @sec-release-three-verdicts (the deceleration the budget assumes).
# │          The contact-force derivation itself lives in
# │          calc-enforcement-contact-force (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact);
# │          this cell reads it through calc-release-contact-premises.
# │ Goal: Restate the handover premises release inherits, and show how little
# │       input error the base's finished budget can absorb at aisle speed.
# │ Show: unbraked force at the free-space TCP limit and at the handover speed;
# │       budget and spare at 1.3 m/s; the delay and the deceleration shortfall
# │       that each consume the spare.
# │ How: contact forces read from EnforcementContactForce (free hand: reduced
# │      mass of hand and arm; clamped: the arm's effective mass alone); the
# │      jerk-limited S-curve stop
# │      (calc_scurve_stop_distance; jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's
# │      peak jerk at the drive limit) and the three overheads; the break-even
# │      deceleration solves v^2/(2a) + v a/(2j) = braking room with j fixed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_stiffness,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    fmt_jerk,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: contact forces, then the budget at aisle speed ────────────────
# Contact premises from the enforcement record (calc-release-contact-premises).
m_eff = EnforcementContactForce.m_eff
f_at_tcp_limit = EnforcementContactForce.f_at_tcp_limit
f_ratio = EnforcementContactForce.f_ratio
f_at_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover
f_at_handover_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_clamped
v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped

# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
c2_braking = calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake).to(meter)
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
d_reaction = (AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay).to(millimeter)
budget_aisle = (d_reaction + c2_braking + overhead_loc + AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
t_spare = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
spare_share = (spare_aisle / AISLE.d_clear).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# Deceleration at which the budget exactly fills the clear distance, jerk bound
# fixed. Above a^2/j the S-curve distance is v^2/(2a) + v a/(2j), so setting it
# equal to the braking room gives (v/(2j)) a^2 - room a + v^2/2 = 0; the smaller
# root is the one on the branch where distance falls as a rises (a < sqrt(v j)).
braking_room = (AISLE.d_clear - AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay - overhead_loc - AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter)
_qa = (AISLE.v_aisle / (2 * j_brake)).to(second**2)
_qc = (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / 2).to(meter**2 / second**2)
a_break_even = ((braking_room - (braking_room**2 - 4 * _qa * _qc) ** 0.5) / (2 * _qa)).to(meter / second**2)
a_shortfall = ((AISLE.a_brake - a_break_even) / AISLE.a_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# Notebook terms (nbk-release-aisle-spare): the two S-curve pieces, the delay
# split, and the dispatch-to-admission allocation Delta_da charged against the
# partial spare (the same allocation @sec-enforcement charges).
d_brake_quad = (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / (2 * AISLE.a_brake)).to(millimeter)
d_brake_jerk = (AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.a_brake / (2 * j_brake)).to(millimeter)
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (allocation of @sec-placement-isolation-decisions)
travel_da = (AISLE.v_aisle * delta_da).to(millimeter)
reserve_aisle = (spare_aisle - travel_da).to(millimeter)
t_reserve = (reserve_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Effective contact mass is 12.0 kg")
check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit")
check(abs(f_ratio - 4.14) < 0.01, "About 4.1x the 50 N criterion")
check(abs(f_at_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N")
check(abs(f_at_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N")
check(f_at_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion < f_at_handover_clamped, "Transient passes, clamped fails the criterion")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Transient handover ceiling is 0.24 m/s")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped handover ceiling is 0.053 m/s")
check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "Jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak")
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "Finished budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Spare spent as delay is 100.8 ms")
# margin_aisle_budget_spare_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types the five terms and the spare
check(abs(d_reaction.magnitude - 173.68) < 5e-3, "Reaction travel 173.7 mm at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(c2_braking.to(millimeter).magnitude - 605.3125) < 5e-3, "S-curve braking 605.3 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Localization allowance 50 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Tracking allowance 40 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.delta_margin.to(millimeter).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Physical margin 100 mm")
check(0.11 < spare_share < 0.125, "The spare is about an eighth of the clear distance")
check(AISLE.v_aisle >= a_break_even**2 / j_brake, "Break-even stop stays in the trapezoidal regime")
check(
    abs((calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, a_break_even, j_brake) - braking_room).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
    "At the break-even deceleration the S-curve stop fills the braking room exactly",
)
check(abs(a_break_even.magnitude - 1.386) < 5e-4, "Break-even deceleration is 1.386 m/s^2")
check(abs(a_shortfall - 0.307) < 5e-4, "A 31 percent deceleration shortfall fills the spare")
check(AISLE.v_aisle >= AISLE.a_brake**2 / j_brake, "Aisle stop is in the trapezoidal regime, so the two-term S-curve form applies")
check(abs((d_brake_quad + d_brake_jerk - c2_braking).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "The two S-curve pieces sum to the braking term")
check(abs(d_brake_quad.magnitude - 422.5) < 5e-3 and abs(d_brake_jerk.magnitude - 182.8125) < 5e-3, "S-curve pieces 422.5 and 182.8 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 1e-9, "Pre-brake delay 133.6 ms")
check(abs((AISLE.perception_age + t_renewal_to_onset - AISLE.tau_delay).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Delay = age + renewal-to-onset")
check(abs(braking_room.to(millimeter).magnitude - 736.32) < 5e-3, "Braking room 736.3 mm")
check(abs(travel_da.magnitude - 82.304) < 5e-3, "Delta_da travel 82.3 mm at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(reserve_aisle.magnitude - 48.7036) < 5e-3, "Reserve 48.7 mm after Delta_da")
check(abs(t_reserve.magnitude - 37.464) < 5e-3, "Reserve 37.5 ms at aisle speed")
check(0 < reserve_aisle < spare_aisle, "Delta_da leaves a positive but smaller reserve")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope:
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_force(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover, precision=1)
    f_handover_clamped_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover_clamped, precision=1)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(round(t_spare.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_break_even_str = fmt_acceleration(a_break_even, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    a_shortfall_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(a_shortfall, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    # Notebook strings (nbk-release-aisle-spare)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    j_brake_str = fmt_jerk(j_brake, unit=meter / second**3, precision=2)
    d_reaction_str = fmt_length(d_reaction, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_brake_quad_str = fmt_length(d_brake_quad, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_brake_jerk_str = fmt_length(d_brake_jerk, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_braking_str = fmt_length(c2_braking, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_loc_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_track_str = fmt_length(AISLE.eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_margin_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_clear_mm_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    braking_room_str = fmt_length(braking_room, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_da_str = fmt_length(travel_da, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    reserve_str = fmt_length(reserve_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_reserve_str = fmt_latency(t_reserve, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    # Budget terms for the margin envelope (generator reads the quantities)
    d_reaction = d_reaction
    d_braking = c2_braking.to(millimeter)
    d_loc = AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter)
    d_track = AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter)
    d_margin = AISLE.delta_margin.to(millimeter)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear.to(millimeter)
    budget = budget_aisle
    spare = spare_aisle
```

The contact criteria arrive as premises from the enforcement record rather than as calculations derived during release review. In @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact, the peak force generated during an unbraked elastic contact with a coworker's hand (@eq-release-unbraked-force) is derived from the arm's effective mass and the standard ISO/TS 15066 biomechanical hand model.[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech] The release case evaluates the operational consequences of those physical results. At the arm's maximum free-space limit of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_tcp_str`, even the transient impact model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_tcp_str`—exceeding the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` criterion by a factor of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_ratio_mult_str`. Consequently, unseparated coworker proximity cannot be permitted at full free-space speed without additional physical containment. When encountering a free hand that recoils upon impact, the criterion admits approach speeds up to `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`, and the chosen handover speed of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str` delivers a safe transient force of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_str`. If the coworker's hand is clamped against a rack upright or structural frame, however, the ceiling drops to `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str`. At that same `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str` approach speed, a clamped collision generates `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_clamped_str`, which breaches the limit. The handover claim is therefore strictly a transient-contact claim, inheriting two essential premises: that the lumped-mass body model and effective mass accurately describe the collision, and that the handover geometry excludes pinching or clamping hazards. Because physical calculations alone cannot guarantee workspace clearance, the release case must establish both premises through empirical evidence and site inspection.

[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech]: **ISO/TS 15066 Values as Case Criteria**\index{ISO/TS 15066!case criterion}: The document supplies a body model and body-region force and pressure data for transient and quasi-static contact [@isots15066]. ISO 10218-2:2025 incorporates the collaborative-application requirements formerly published as ISO/TS 15066; ISO/TS 15066:2016 itself remains published and is under revision [@iso10218part2]. The `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` handover criterion is none of those tabulated values and not an injury boundary; the site assessment chooses it for one body region, contact type, and geometry, so a change to any of the three reopens the claim instead of inheriting its margin.

Unlike the arm's instantaneous force criteria, the mobile base's claim is an integrated distance budget. Validating this claim requires empirical evidence bounding the perception observation age, communication bus latencies, and execution lease durations. The stopping budget integrates @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope with the jerk-limited $C^2$ braking profile from @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget). In deployment authorization, the critical engineering metric is the margin of clear distance that remains unspent (\ref{nbk-release-aisle-spare}).

::: {#nbk-release-aisle-spare .callout-notebook title="The aisle spare"}

**Problem**: At the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, how much of the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance does the stopping budget leave unspent, what error in a single input would spend it, and how much remains once dispatch-to-admission work is charged?

**Variables**:

- Aisle speed $v =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (Chosen); clear distance $D_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` (Illustrative, standing in for a site survey)
- Pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.tau_delay_str` (Derived from illustrative terms: `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_age_str` observation age plus `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_renewal_to_onset_str` from the last valid renewal to brake onset)
- Credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` (Illustrative) and jerk bound $j =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.j_brake_str` (Derived, @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
- Allowances $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_loc_str` and $\epsilon_{\text{track}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_track_str` (Illustrative); margin $\delta_{\text{margin}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_margin_str` (Chosen)
- Dispatch-to-admission allocation $\Delta_{\text{da}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.delta_da_str` (Illustrative allocation, @sec-placement-isolation-decisions)

**Math**:

1. **Reaction**: $v\,\tau_{\text{delay}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` $\times$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.tau_delay_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_reaction_str`.
2. **Braking**: Because $v \ge a_{\text{brake}}^2/j$, the stop reaches full deceleration, and $v^2/(2a_{\text{brake}}) + v\,a_{\text{brake}}/(2j) =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_brake_quad_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_brake_jerk_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_braking_str`.
3. **Spare**: `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_reaction_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_braking_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_loc_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_track_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_margin_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str`, leaving `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_mm_str` $-$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str`.
4. **One input wrong**: As extra delay, `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` $/$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_spare_str`. As weaker braking, setting step 2 equal to the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.braking_room_str` braking room gives $a =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_break_even_str`, a `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` shortfall.
5. **Admission charged**: $v\,\Delta_{\text{da}} =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` $\times$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.delta_da_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.travel_da_str`, leaving a reserve of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.reserve_str`, or `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_reserve_str` at aisle speed.

**Result**: The budget spends all but `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` of the clear distance before admission work, and all but `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.reserve_str` after it.

**Systems insight**: The validity of the stopping guarantee $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ hinges on the narrow margin of unspent distance rather than the nominal distance consumed. Because every operational uncertainty erodes this thin reserve, an overestimation of achievable deceleration by just `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` completely exhausts the stopping margin.

:::

This reserve must also absorb any unmodeled runtime uncertainties, meaning it cannot simply be treated as extra allowable latency or repurposed as a margin for control handovers (@sec-intervention-authority-transitions). If an engineering team fails to empirically measure each component of the timing and kinematic chain, they cannot prove that this razor-thin reserve will survive the compounding latencies and friction variances encountered on a production floor.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_aisle_budget_spare_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal stacked bar in millimeters: reaction travel of 173.7 millimeters, braking of 605.3 millimeters, then allowances of 50 for localization, 40 for tracking, and 100 millimeters of physical margin, followed by a dashed box for the 131.0 millimeters spare that ends at a red line marking the 1.10 meters clear distance."}

*The partial budget leaves only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` of the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance spare.*
:::

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, deployment authorization resolves into three verifiable physical criteria: the mobile base must halt within the surveyed clear distance, the manipulator must unlatch the access door below the allowable mechanical force limit, and item handovers must strictly respect human biomechanical force boundaries. Each inequality depends directly on verified assumptions regarding achievable deceleration, sensor-to-actuator latency, and contact stiffness. Because these physical properties can degrade over mechanical operating life, an auditable safety case must lay bare these runtime dependencies, allowing certification engineers to rigorously evaluate whether the empirical evidence supports deployment.
## Safety Cases and Claims {#sec-release-safety-cases-claims}

A photograph of a clear aisle cannot establish that a loaded mobile base will stop before reaching an obstacle. A valid stopping claim depends on guaranteed physical clearance, actual braking capability, and end-to-end response timing, with each parameter supported by empirical evidence gathered under documented operational conditions. A safety case systematically links these physical premises to the release claim, enabling an assessor to verify which guarantees are empirically supported and which remain unvalidated.

### Assurance argument grammar and warrants {#sec-release-assurance-grammar}

A safety case is auditable only when its logical structure is written down in a format that another engineer can inspect and challenge link by link. Two notations are widely used in practice, and both capture the same underlying assurance structure. The **claim-argument-evidence (CAE)**\index{Claim-argument-evidence!notation} framework divides the argument into three distinct elements: the *claim*, an assertion about system behavior that is either true or false; the *argument*, the causal or inductive reasoning connecting the claim to empirical observations; and the *evidence*, the calibrated measurements and test artifacts themselves [@bishop1998methodology; @bloomfield2014building]. **Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!elements} expresses the identical structure as a directed graph: top-level goals (claims) decompose through explicit strategies (arguments) into concrete solutions (evidence items), while context and assumption nodes define the operational envelope within which each link remains valid [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal]. The fault injection records from @sec-verification-contract-matrix enter this graph directly as solutions, supporting each named sub-claim. Because release adjudication turns an assurance graph into a binding operational authorization, the safety case defined in \ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!argument structure} evaluates directly to an enforceable release verdict.

This structural decomposition descends from Stephen Toulmin's foundational model of practical argumentation[^fn-toulmin-argument-anatomy] [@toulmin1958uses]. In industrial practice, standards such as ANSI/UL 4600 mandate goal-based safety cases for autonomous physical products [@ul4600; @koopman2023ul4600]. Production autonomous fleets employ this exact paradigm; for example, Waymo structures the safety case for its driverless ride-hailing operations around layered, dynamic claims demonstrating the absence of unreasonable risk, arguing separately that its risk acceptance criteria are comprehensive and that their empirical evaluation is trustworthy [@favaro2023building]. For an embodied robotic system, the root claim $C_0$ defines a testable physical invariant—such as guaranteeing that stopping distance remains within surveyed aisle clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) or limiting collaborative contact force ($F_{\text{contact}} \le F_{\text{limit}}$). Supporting sub-claims delineate the necessary mechanical, electrical, and computational conditions, and retained test records substantiate each leaf. Formulating these relationships as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) prevents circular reasoning and exposes intermediate dependencies: a reviewer can trace any operational assertion directly down to supporting physical observations and operating assumptions.

[^fn-toulmin-argument-anatomy]: **Toulmin's Argument Anatomy**\index{Toulmin, Stephen!argument model}: *The Uses of Argument* [@toulmin1958uses] splits practical reasoning into claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal. Safety cases preserve this anatomy: evidence supplies the data, stated confidence acts as the qualifier, and the rebuttal becomes the defeater evaluated during adversarial review (@sec-release-adversarial-review).

::: {#dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case .callout-definition title="Claim-argument-evidence safety case"}

***Claim-argument-evidence safety case***\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!definition}\index{Safety case!physical AI} is a structured argument that a named machine, in a stated operating envelope and under a stated fault model, meets explicit physical criteria, written as claims that decompose through stated arguments into retained evidence.

1.  **Significance**: It makes a release decision checkable one link at a time. For the warehouse machine, the three inequalities of @eq-release-authorization-criterion become six claims whose leaves are individual premises, and a reviewer can find the one premise, such as a braking deceleration no loaded trial has measured, on which the verdict turns.
2.  **Distinction**: A test report or benchmark score records what happened under the conditions sampled. A safety case states why that evidence supports a claim about conditions the machine has not yet met, and names the assumptions under which the reasoning stops holding.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that the case is paperwork assembled after development for a regulator. It is written with the design, and in this book's architecture its verdict decides what the permission path lets the machine do.

:::

The structural integrity of this engineering assertion DAG hinges on strictly distinguishing evidence from demonstration. A **demonstration**\index{Demonstration!vs. evidence} records successful task execution across an uncharacterized test distribution—such as a series of clean door openings with the strike plate at its nominal position, or a thousand collision-free warehouse transits. Demonstrations quantify nominal empirical performance across observed runs, but they yield no mathematical or statistical bounds on tail distributions, sensor corruptions, or corner cases outside the logged trajectories. In contrast, evidence consists of falsifiable, calibrated artifacts with quantified uncertainty bounds: an execution-time distribution measured on a hardware logic analyzer paired with formal worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds, loaded vehicle stopping trials conducted across degraded friction surfaces, or hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) fault-injection traces testing boundary conditions. Evidence requirements correspond directly to the scope of the claim. Nominal trials adequately support nominal capability assertions, and calibration logs validate sensor coordinate frames. However, establishing an envelope boundary or worst-case response requires exhaustive coverage, quantified uncertainty margins, and a rigorous warrant.

Connecting evidence to a claim requires a **warrant**\index{Warrant!inferential rule}—the inferential principle explaining why empirical data validate an operational assertion. For a learned neural policy, engineers often invoke an inductive warrant, reasoning from thousands of failure-free test episodes to infer future operational reliability. Yet the exposure wall analyzed in @sec-evaluation-trial-limits demonstrates why purely inductive warrants cannot support catastrophic hazard claims. Under the Poisson zero-event rule ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), statistically proving an ultra-reliable failure rate of $10^{-9}$ per operating hour requires billions of operating hours without a single failure [@butler1993infeasibility; @kalra2016driving]. Determining an acceptable target rate in the first place is an engineering and societal judgment that empirical testing cannot establish on its own [@koopman2022how].

A defensible safety case bridges this gap through deterministic architectural warrants. Rather than betting physical safety on policy generalization, the system grounds its top-level safety claims in an independent permission path (@sec-enforcement). This monitor evaluates Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to clamp actuator commands and command an assessed safe stop whenever a learned proposal approaches the boundary of the viable set $\mathcal{C}_{\text{viable}}$. Crucially, this architectural warrant bounds and narrows the claim rather than magically evading physical limits: the permission path protects only against monitored hazards that the actuators can physically arrest within the available stopping clearance (@sec-frontier-shield-dilution). The learned proposer still requires its own operational argument to demonstrate functional capability and handle non-monitored tasks. Emerging standards formalize these complementary roles: ISO/PAS 8800:2024 adapts automotive safety lifecycles, data curation requirements, and assurance arguments to AI components [@iso8800], while the Assurance of Machine Learning in Autonomous Systems (AMLAS) framework provides structured safety-case patterns for machine learning pipelines across general autonomous systems [@hawkins2021amlas]. In this book's architecture, the permission path shoulders the safety argument for all monitored physical hazards—anchoring its formal claims to rated watchdogs, certified drive functions, and safety-rated laser scanners (@sec-release-standards-map)—freeing the learned proposer's assurance argument to focus on operational availability and unmonitored mission tasks.

### Contextual assumptions and the weakest link {#sec-release-contextual-assumptions}

Every physical measurement carries tacit environmental dependencies. A vehicle stopping test conducted on clean, dry concrete under bright industrial lighting depends intimately on those ambient conditions. Transferring that machine into a dimly lit aisle can drastically increase perception latency and observation age, even when the mechanical brakes and tires behave identically. An assurance argument must make these contextual assumptions explicit, ensuring that empirical evidence gathered under one set of conditions is never invalidly applied outside its verified operating envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-low-light-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AN UNSTATED LIGHTING ASSUMPTION IN THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (contextual-assumptions paragraph).
# │ Goal: Show how a lighting change the budget never named ages the navigation
# │       camera's image, and what it would cost the aisle budget's spare
# │       if the age check did not refuse the frames.
# │ Show: nominal and low-light exposure, the added observation age, the added
# │       travel at aisle speed, and its share of the spare.
# │ How: perception age is timed from mid-exposure (AISLE.perception_age), so a
# │      longer exposure adds half its increase; spare from the jerk-limited
# │      S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance; jerk bound = the reference C2
# │      polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit) and the three overheads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
low_light_exposure_factor = 2.0  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption: a dim aisle doubles the exposure)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_exp_nominal = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
t_exp_low = (low_light_exposure_factor * t_exp_nominal).to(millisecond)
dt_age = ((t_exp_low - t_exp_nominal) / 2).to(millisecond)  # mid-exposure timestamp
d_added = (AISLE.v_aisle * dt_age).to(millimeter)
# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
budget = (
    AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay
    + calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake)
    + AISLE.delta_loc
    + AISLE.eps_track
    + AISLE.delta_margin
).to(millimeter)
spare = (AISLE.d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
share_of_spare = (d_added / spare).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_exp_nominal.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, "Navigation-camera exposure 16 ms")
check(abs(dt_age.magnitude - 8.0) < 1e-9, "Low light adds 8 ms of observation age")
check(abs(d_added.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-9, "10.4 mm of added travel at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(share_of_spare - 0.079) < 5e-3, "About 8 percent of the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseLowLight:
    t_exp_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_nominal, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_low_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_low, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dt_age_str = fmt_latency(dt_age, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_added_str = fmt_length(d_added, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    share_str = fmt_percent(round(share_of_spare * 100) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

When an operating assumption is left unstated, safety depends entirely on whether a downstream check happens to catch the resulting deviation. In our mobile manipulator's stopping budget, the warrant quietly assumes that warehouse illumination permits the navigation camera to operate at its nominal exposure. If dim lighting doubles that exposure time from `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_nominal_str` to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_low_str`, the observation arrives `{python} ReleaseLowLight.dt_age_str` older than assumed (measuring exposure age from mid-frame). Left unchecked, this additional latency translates to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.d_added_str` of extra travel at the robot's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.v_aisle_str` aisle velocity, consuming roughly `{python} ReleaseLowLight.share_str` of the budget's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.spare_str` margin. Fortunately, the permission path's frame admission age check rejects these delayed frames. However, because an active motion chunk can execute only while its underlying evidence and lease remain valid, the robot halts unexpectedly in an aisle where the design assumed it could operate smoothly. The engineering team experiences this unstated lighting assumption not as an immediate collision, but as baffling availability failures—and only a latency check unconnected to illumination kept that blind spot from eroding physical clearance.

Assumptions that lack runtime monitors carry far greater danger. Mechanical drift in a camera mount can introduce steady-state calibration offsets while every frame passes freshness and timestamp validations. The safety case must explicitly link localization tolerances to calibration routines and physical inspection logs. Treating fresh telemetry as proof of accurate spatial calibration leaves that critical warrant completely unsupported.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Epistemic assumptions embedded within safety case warrants are critically interrogated in @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-argument-confidence
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HOW CONFIDENCE COMBINES IN A SAFETY ARGUMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-contextual-assumptions (the conjunctive and
# │          multi-legged argument paragraphs).
# │ Goal: Show that doubt accumulates across required premises, and that two
# │       independent legs can support a claim better than either leg alone.
# │ Show: confidence in a conjunction of n required premises; confidence in a
# │       claim supported by either of two independent legs.
# │ How: independent premises; conjunction = product of confidences
# │      (calc_conjunctive_confidence); two independent legs fail together
# │      with probability (1-p1)(1-p2) (calc_multilegged_confidence).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics import calc_conjunctive_confidence, calc_multilegged_confidence
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

# ┌── 1. LOAD: chapter-local inputs (a teaching illustration, not a machine value)
p_premise = 0.99  # category: illustrative (confidence in each required premise)
n_premises = 10  # category: illustrative (number of required premises)
p_leg = 0.90  # category: illustrative (confidence in each of two independent legs)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
p_conjunction = calc_conjunctive_confidence([p_premise] * n_premises)
p_two_legs = calc_multilegged_confidence([p_leg, p_leg])

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(p_conjunction - 0.904) < 5e-4, "Ten premises at 0.99 give about 0.90")
check(p_conjunction < p_premise, "The conjunction is weaker than its weakest premise")
check(abs(p_two_legs - 0.99) < 1e-9, "Two independent legs at 0.90 give 0.99")
check(p_two_legs > p_leg, "Independent legs support the claim better than either leg")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseArgumentConfidence:
    p_premise_str = fmt(p_premise, precision=2)
    n_premises_str = fmt(n_premises, precision=0)
    p_conjunction_str = fmt(round(p_conjunction, 2), precision=2)
    p_leg_str = fmt(p_leg, precision=2)
    p_two_legs_str = fmt(round(p_two_legs, 2), precision=2)
```

A safety case is not an aggregate scorecard in which high performance in one branch compensates for a deficit in another. Benchmark accuracy on an object recognition dataset cannot offset an uncharacterized latency tail on a CAN FD (Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate) bus, nor can millions of simulated training episodes compensate for missing brake-wear measurements. When every child claim is *required*, the argument is conjunctive: it is no stronger than its weakest required premise. In practice it is usually weaker, because doubt across independent premises accumulates. For $n$ independent required premises held with confidences $p_1, \dots, p_n$, confidence in the root claim $C$ is their product:
$$P(C) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i.$$ {#eq-release-conjunctive-confidence}

If each of `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.n_premises_str` required premises holds with confidence `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_premise_str`, the overall conjunction holds with only about `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_conjunction_str`—a confidence lower than that of any individual premise. The mobile base's stopping claim exemplifies this conjunctive fragility: surveyed clear distance, credible braking deceleration, brake onset latency, observation age, and localization and tracking tolerances all enter a single stopping budget. A flawed warrant in any single term invalidates the root claim, regardless of how thoroughly the other terms are documented. An assessor therefore focuses not on the gross volume of supporting documentation, but on the least supported required premise and the number of premises sharing the claim.

This conjunctive degradation has one principled engineering exception.
